questions.question: A retail website runs on EC2 instances behind an ALB. Server load surges without warning during flash sales and sits nearly idle overnight. The operations team wants to eliminate overnight idle costs while absorbing unpredictable sales spikes without manual intervention. Which compute strategy achieves this?
options: Pre-scale with Scheduled Scaling set to business hours on weekdays
Configure an Auto Scaling Group with a CPU target tracking policy at 60%
Run the entire fleet on Spot Instances with a mixed-instance allocation strategy across pools
Operate a fixed peak-sized fleet on 1-year Reserved Instances and accept the overnight idle
questions.explanation: Target-tracking auto-scaling adjusts fleet size to keep average CPU near the configured target, shrinking the fleet overnight to cut idle spend and adding instances reactively when a flash sale arrives — no calendar pre-knowledge required. Scheduled Scaling fires on a fixed calendar trigger; flash sales that hit outside the configured window will overwhelm an under-provisioned fleet. A pure Spot fleet (even with a mixed-instance allocation strategy) is subject to capacity reclamation with two minutes' notice during demand surges — exactly when the retail checkout must stay up. A fixed Reserved-Instance fleet sized for peak removes auto-scaling entirely, leaving the overnight idle cost the team explicitly wanted to eliminate.

questions.question: An online gaming platform stores a real-time leaderboard mapping player IDs to scores and ranks. During peak tournament events, the service handles 600,000 read operations per minute and every lookup is by a single player ID — no aggregations or joins are required. Response latency must stay under 5 milliseconds as player count is expected to triple over the next year. Which AWS database service is the best fit?
options: Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity mode
Amazon Aurora MySQL with a Multi-AZ standby and provisioned IOPS
Amazon Redshift with result-set caching enabled for repeated queries
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached used as the authoritative data store
questions.explanation: DynamoDB is purpose-built for high-throughput, low-latency key lookups at any scale — on-demand capacity automatically adjusts to handle unpredictable peak volumes without manual provisioning, and single-digit millisecond performance is maintained regardless of table size. Aurora MySQL is a relational engine optimized for transactional queries with joins; matching DynamoDB's sub-5ms key-lookup latency at 600k requests/minute requires significant tuning overhead and dedicated read replicas, making it a poor fit for this simple, high-volume access pattern. Redshift is an OLAP data warehouse designed for analytical scans across large datasets, not single-key point lookups at low latency. ElastiCache for Memcached is an in-memory cache without durability — data is lost on node restart or eviction, making it unsuitable as the authoritative store for a leaderboard that must persist through failures.

questions.question: An application stores user-uploaded files in S3. Files are frequently accessed for the first 30 days, rarely accessed for the next 60 days, then never needed again. Which S3 lifecycle configuration minimizes storage cost?
options: S3 Standard with no lifecycle policy, retaining objects for all 90+ days indefinitely
Store all objects in S3 Glacier Deep Archive from day 1 — including the first 30 days
Transition to S3 Standard-IA at day 30; expire at 90 days total
Apply S3 Intelligent-Tiering across all 90 days to auto-manage storage class
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA charges lower per-GB storage rates than Standard but adds a per-GB retrieval fee — an ideal trade-off once objects transition from frequent to infrequent access after day 30. Expiring objects at day 90 eliminates ongoing cost for data that will never be needed again. Keeping all 90+ days in S3 Standard pays the premium tier even after access frequency drops to near-zero. Glacier Deep Archive from day 1 imposes up to 12-hour retrieval delays during the first 30 days when files are frequently accessed — retrieval latency and fees during that window outweigh the storage savings. S3 Intelligent-Tiering adds a per-object monitoring fee that is wasted here because the access pattern is already known and a deterministic lifecycle transition is cheaper.

questions.question: An e-commerce site runs EC2 instances behind an ALB, with all instances in a single subnet in us-east-1a. During an AWS maintenance event affecting that Availability Zone, the application returns 503 errors for 40 minutes. The architecture team must ensure no future single-AZ event causes a full outage. What change addresses the root cause?
options: Enable a second AZ on the ALB and distribute the Auto Scaling Group across us-east-1a and us-east-1b
Reduce the ALB health-check interval to 5 s and enable EC2 Auto Recovery to restart failed instances
Build a second-Region failover stack in us-west-2 with Route 53 health-check-driven DNS failover
Take cross-AZ EBS snapshots every 15 minutes and restore into us-east-1b after the next outage detected
questions.explanation: Spreading the Auto Scaling Group across two AZs and enabling both AZs on the ALB ensures the load balancer keeps routing traffic to healthy targets in the surviving zone when the other zone is impaired — the minimum change that removes the single-AZ dependency. EC2 Auto Recovery only restarts a failed instance on healthy hardware inside the same Availability Zone, so it cannot help when the entire AZ is impaired. A second-Region failover stack is overkill for a single-AZ fault domain and adds cross-region replication and DNS-TTL complexity the question does not call for. Cross-AZ EBS snapshots still require an operator-driven restore and instance launch during the outage window, making RTO unpredictable and far worse than an automated multi-AZ topology.

questions.question: A DevOps engineer discovers that an EC2 web application is calling S3 using access keys stored in a plaintext configuration file on the instance. The security team requires these long-lived credentials to be removed immediately while preserving S3 read access. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create a dedicated IAM user, deploy its credentials to the instance via environment variables
Store the credentials as SecureString parameters in SSM and pull them on each instance boot
Rotate the access keys and redeploy the instance image with updated credential values
Attach an IAM role to the instance and remove all hard-coded access keys
questions.explanation: Attaching an IAM role to an EC2 instance causes the instance metadata service (IMDS) to vend temporary, automatically-rotated credentials — no static keys exist on the instance to be stolen or leaked, and the application calls S3 using the same SDK with no code change. Creating a dedicated IAM user and shipping its access keys via environment variables simply moves the same long-lived secret to a different filesystem location; the credential is still static and leakable. SSM SecureString parameters are KMS-encrypted at rest, but the long-lived IAM-user key inside the parameter is still a static credential that must be rotated manually. Rotating and redeploying the keys reduces the exposure window but does not eliminate the fundamental static-credential risk the security team flagged.

questions.question: A SaaS company's CRM application uses Amazon RDS MySQL as its primary database. A newly deployed analytics dashboard runs complex GROUP BY queries across three years of interaction records, pushing primary instance CPU to 90% during business hours and causing response time degradation for transactional users. Writes must continue on the primary without interruption. Which solution isolates the analytics workload without affecting transactional performance?
options: Add an RDS Read Replica and point the analytics dashboard at the replica endpoint
Upgrade the primary instance to absorb the dashboard workload alongside transactional traffic
Route the dashboard's analytics queries to the Multi-AZ standby's read-only endpoint
Enable RDS Performance Insights and auto-terminate slow dashboard queries
questions.explanation: An RDS Read Replica receives asynchronous replication from the primary and exposes a separate endpoint — heavy analytics queries run against the replica, leaving primary CPU available for transactional writes with no schema changes. Upgrading the primary instance class adds raw CPU headroom but does not isolate the two workloads: a 40-second analytics scan still competes with transactional queries for shared CPU and I/O, and the headroom erodes as data volume grows. The Multi-AZ standby is a synchronous failover replica maintained for HA only; it does not accept query traffic and has no addressable read endpoint. Performance Insights surfaces slow queries but auto-terminating them breaks the analytics dashboard rather than isolating it.

questions.question: A startup's production environment has web servers in public subnets and application servers in private subnets. After migrating to a newly created VPC, the application servers can no longer download software patches from the internet, although they receive no inbound connections. What change should the solutions architect make?
options: Update the private subnet route table to forward 0.0.0.0/0 to the existing Internet Gateway in the public subnet
Add a VPC peering connection to a transit VPC whose public subnet has internet access
Allocate an Elastic IP and a public IP alias to each application server in the private subnet
Deploy a NAT Gateway in the public subnet and update the private subnet route table to send 0.0.0.0/0 to it
questions.explanation: A NAT Gateway placed in a public subnet uses the subnet's Internet Gateway to make outbound connections on behalf of private-subnet resources, translating source addresses so replies route back correctly. Private instances initiate the connection but remain unreachable from the internet because they have no public IP and no inbound route. Pointing the private subnet's default route at the existing Internet Gateway fails because private-subnet instances lack public IPs — the Internet Gateway drops outbound packets that have no valid public source address to translate against. A VPC peering connection extends Layer-3 reachability between VPCs but does not provide internet egress on its own; peering traffic is never transitive through another VPC's IGW. Allocating an Elastic IP to each instance in a private subnet still requires a route to an Internet Gateway and exposes those instances to inbound internet traffic, defeating the private-subnet design.

questions.question: A global software vendor needs to publish product documentation, images, and downloadable PDFs for a product launch microsite. The 3 GB file set is updated roughly once per month and must load quickly for visitors across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. The team has no dedicated server administrators and must minimize both cost and ongoing operational effort. Which architecture meets these requirements?
options: Host the assets in S3 and distribute them through a CloudFront distribution with edge caching
Deploy file-serving EC2 instances in three regions behind Route 53 latency-based routing with Auto Scaling
Use Elastic Beanstalk to run a Node.js server that reads assets from an Amazon EFS volume
Place files in S3 and expose them through an Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled
questions.explanation: S3 provides durable, serverless object storage with no servers to patch or scale, and CloudFront distributes content from hundreds of edge locations so visitors worldwide receive files from the nearest point of presence — achieving sub-100 ms load times with no compute to operate. Multi-region EC2 with latency-based DNS achieves geographic proximity but requires capacity planning, OS patching, Auto Scaling configuration, and 24/7 operations in each region — directly violating the 'no dedicated administrators' constraint. Elastic Beanstalk running a Node.js server in front of EFS introduces a single-region compute tier and per-server filesystem latency, neither of which gives global users edge proximity. An Application Load Balancer cannot use S3 as a native origin, performs no edge caching, and would still require backend compute to serve the files.

questions.question: A security audit finds that a Lambda function processing payment records connects to an RDS PostgreSQL database using the publicly accessible endpoint. The security team requires the database to be unreachable from the internet while Lambda retains the ability to execute queries. What configuration achieves this?
options: Remove RDS public access and restrict connections via a security policy scoped to Lambda's execution role
Create a VPC peering connection and a security group that routes Lambda traffic into the private RDS subnet
Deploy Lambda inside the VPC and configure the RDS security group to allow access from the Lambda security group
Keep RDS publicly accessible, harden the network security group, and rotate credentials hourly via Secrets Manager
questions.explanation: Configuring Lambda with VPC settings creates an ENI in the specified subnets, allowing Lambda to reach RDS over private IP addresses — no public endpoint required. Disabling RDS public accessibility ensures no internet-originating connection can reach the database. Removing public access and relying on an execution-role 'security policy' does not work because RDS network access is governed by VPC security groups, not by IAM roles attached to the caller. VPC peering connects two VPCs at the network layer but cannot bridge a public-only Lambda to a private subnet — Lambda must still have an ENI in a routable VPC to use private addressing. Keeping RDS publicly accessible with a hardened security group and hourly credential rotation still leaves a reachable internet endpoint, violating the explicit requirement.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform's order service publishes completed orders to three independent downstream systems — inventory management, shipping fulfillment, and customer email — each of which must process every order event. The engineering team requires that adding a new consumer needs no changes to the order service. Which AWS pattern achieves this?
options: Write directly to each downstream service's individual SQS queue from the order service
Publish to an SNS topic; each service subscribes via its own SQS queue
Store orders in DynamoDB Streams and configure each consumer to react to item changes
Route orders to a Kinesis Data Stream; each downstream service reads from a dedicated shard
questions.explanation: The SNS fan-out pattern decouples the producer from consumers completely — the order service publishes once to a topic, and each SQS-subscribed service receives an independent copy automatically. Adding a new consumer requires only a new SNS subscription, with zero changes to the order service. Writing directly to each downstream SQS queue creates N point-to-point dependencies — when a new consumer is added, the order-service code must be updated to write to the additional queue, violating the decoupling requirement. DynamoDB Streams emits item-change events tied to a table, not a message bus, and adding new consumers means re-implementing every downstream as a stream consumer with shard-iteration logic. Kinesis with one shard per service does not fan out the same record — each shard holds a distinct subset of data, so a single order event is not delivered to every consumer.

questions.question: A financial services firm transfers 4 TB of market-data feeds per day from its co-located on-premises data center to Amazon S3 in us-east-1. The architecture team requires consistent, predictable throughput of at least 1 Gbps. Compliance policy mandates that data must not traverse the public internet. The firm already has a cross-connect available at a colocation facility. Which connectivity solution satisfies all three requirements?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration over public CloudFront edges, sized for a 1 Gbps sustained colocation upload
AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the corporate internet with a 1 Gbps tunnel from the colocation cross-connect
AWS Direct Connect with a 1 Gbps circuit terminating at the colocation cross-connect
AWS Client VPN at the colocation site with split tunneling and a 1 Gbps cross-connect to AWS
questions.explanation: Direct Connect provisions a private physical circuit between the on-premises data center and AWS over the existing colocation cross-connect, providing guaranteed bandwidth entirely outside the public internet — the only option that simultaneously satisfies the throughput, predictability, and no-public-internet requirements. S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront edge locations over the public internet, failing the compliance mandate and offering no throughput guarantee. Site-to-Site VPN is an IPsec tunnel that terminates on public AWS endpoints; even with BGP routing, traffic crosses the public internet, violating the same mandate. AWS Client VPN is a remote-access service for individual user endpoints, not a site-to-AWS data transport, and it also terminates on a public endpoint.

questions.question: A company runs a compliance archival system where regulatory documents are uploaded once and retrieved at most once per year for audits. The compliance team's primary constraint is storage cost, not retrieval speed. Which S3 storage class is most appropriate?
options: S3 Standard-IA — millisecond reads, $0.0125/GB-month plus retrieval fee
S3 One Zone-IA — single AZ, lower redundancy, millisecond access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — 12-hour retrieval, $0.00099/GB-month
S3 Standard — multi-AZ, immediate access, $0.023/GB-month
questions.explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class at roughly $0.00099 per GB-month, designed for data accessed at most once or twice per year with retrieval time up to 12 hours. For annual compliance audits where retrieval latency is irrelevant, this is the cost-optimal choice. S3 Standard costs roughly 23× more per GB and provides immediate retrieval that the workload does not need. Standard-IA still costs more per GB than Glacier and charges a per-retrieval fee that hurts when auditors pull large object sets at once. One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA but still far more expensive than Deep Archive and sacrifices multi-AZ durability without offering archival-tier pricing.

questions.question: A financial application processes wire transfer instructions from an SQS queue using a Lambda function. After a code deployment, certain message formats cause the Lambda function to throw an unhandled exception. These messages are returned to the queue, immediately retried, and continue failing — consuming Lambda invocations while delaying valid messages. What should the solutions architect implement?
options: Configure a Dead Letter Queue with maxReceiveCount=3 and a CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth
Switch the source queue to FIFO so wire transfers are processed in strict order with the same retry policy
Increase the visibility timeout to 5 minutes so Lambda has more time to process each message
Extend the message retention period to 14 days so failing messages are not deleted automatically
questions.explanation: A Dead Letter Queue receives messages that exceed maxReceiveCount processing attempts, permanently removing them from the main queue so they stop consuming Lambda invocations and blocking healthy traffic. A CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth alerts the team when failures accumulate, enabling rapid root-cause investigation. Switching to a FIFO source preserves message order but does nothing to stop a poison-pill message from cycling endlessly — strict ordering actually makes the problem worse, because a single failing message halts every later message in the same MessageGroupId. Increasing the visibility timeout just delays each retry; the bad message still cycles back once the timeout expires. Extending retention to 14 days lengthens the failure window rather than terminating it.

questions.question: A horizontally scaled web tier runs across multiple EC2 instances behind an ALB. Users intermittently report being logged out when the ALB routes them to a different instance. Investigation reveals each instance stores session data in local process memory. What is the most operationally simple fix that also survives instance replacement?
options: Enable sticky sessions on the ALB to route each user to the same instance
Persist each instance's session data to its local EBS volume
Move session storage to a shared ElastiCache Redis cluster
Store sessions in DynamoDB and query the session table on each request
questions.explanation: Storing sessions in an external ElastiCache Redis cluster makes session data accessible from any instance in the fleet — a new or replacement instance can immediately retrieve any user's session without interruption, and Multi-AZ mode keeps Redis available even during a primary node failure. Sticky sessions stop the immediate routing problem but do not fix durability: when the pinned instance is replaced during a deployment or failure, every user session bound to that instance is lost simultaneously, producing a worse batch-logout event than the original complaint. Persisting sessions to each instance's EBS volume still ties session data to one specific instance — EBS volumes do not follow a replaced instance and are inaccessible from any other instance in the ASG. DynamoDB can store sessions but requires per-request reads against an external service, adding latency on every page view and per-call cost that Redis avoids.

questions.question: A company needs to migrate 50 TB of data to S3. Their internet connection is 100 Mbps and is needed for business operations. The data must be transferred within 5 days. Which service should they use?
options: AWS Snowball Edge shipped to the data center and physically returned to AWS
AWS DataSync agent over the existing 100 Mbps link with incremental sync enabled
S3 Transfer Acceleration tuned for parallel multipart uploads of every file
A new AWS Direct Connect 1 Gbps port provisioned and used to push the 50 TB in a single window
questions.explanation: 50 TB over a 100 Mbps link takes roughly 46 days at full utilization — and the link must keep serving the business, so it cannot be saturated. Snowball Edge bypasses the link entirely: data is loaded onto the device locally and shipped to AWS for ingest into S3, comfortably inside the 5-day window. DataSync optimizes file-level transfers and supports incremental sync, but it still runs through the same 100 Mbps pipe and hits the same calendar wall. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads via CloudFront edges, but the local pipe remains the bottleneck. A new Direct Connect port takes weeks to provision (cross-connect order + LOA-CFA + circuit turn-up), making it impossible to complete within 5 days.

questions.question: A financial reporting service writes an account balance to DynamoDB and immediately performs a read to return the updated value to the client. Testers consistently observe stale values — the read returns the pre-update balance. The development team wants to fix this in code without changing the table design or data model. What change should they make?
options: Set ConsistentRead=true on every GetItem and Query call against the table
Switch table reads to a Global Secondary Index scoped to the account partition
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table for cached reads
Replace GetItem with a Query that uses a FilterExpression on the balance attribute of the same table
questions.explanation: Setting ConsistentRead=true forces DynamoDB to read from the partition's leader node and return data that reflects all writes acknowledged before the read, eliminating the stale-read window that exists under eventually consistent (default) mode. Switching reads to a Global Secondary Index makes the situation worse — GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads at all, regardless of the ConsistentRead flag. DAX caches reads in memory and would also worsen the problem; it would serve the cached pre-update value until its TTL expires rather than the freshly written value. Replacing GetItem with a Query that uses a FilterExpression still reads the base table with the same default consistency, so stale results remain possible.

questions.question: A media sharing platform lets users upload large video files from a browser. Currently all uploads pass through the application server tier before being written to S3, creating bandwidth bottlenecks and high EC2 costs during peak hours. The security team requires that upload credentials expire no more than 15 minutes after issuance. Which solution removes the application server from the upload data path while meeting the security requirement?
options: Deploy AWS Transfer Family with SFTP fronting the application fleet to handle every browser upload at scale
Route every upload through API Gateway as a binary passthrough that the application server still proxies internally
Open the S3 bucket for public PUT access and rely on a static 15-minute token shared with the browser
Have the application server return a 15-minute presigned S3 PUT URL so the browser uploads directly
questions.explanation: A presigned PUT URL embeds the uploader's identity and expiry into a signed request URL. The application server generates the URL without ever touching file bytes, hands it to the browser, and the browser PUTs the file straight to S3 — eliminating the EC2 bandwidth bottleneck. Setting the URL TTL to 15 minutes satisfies the credential-lifetime requirement. AWS Transfer Family fronting the existing fleet still terminates uploads on the same EC2 instances, so the bottleneck remains. API Gateway as a binary passthrough imposes a 10 MB request-body cap and re-introduces a server hop for every byte. Public PUT access on the bucket violates least privilege and lets any URL holder overwrite arbitrary objects.

questions.question: A company has grown to 15 AWS accounts across different business units. The security team requires that all outbound traffic to the internet pass through a single inspection point before leaving AWS. A solutions architect must design the network topology to enforce this without deploying redundant NAT infrastructure in every account. What is the recommended approach?
options: Set up AWS PrivateLink from each spoke account to a centralized proxy service
Deploy full-mesh VPC peering between all 15 accounts and route through shared NAT
Attach a Transit Gateway to all accounts with a shared egress VPC at the center
Provision a NAT Gateway in each account and centralize logs in Security Hub
questions.explanation: AWS Transit Gateway acts as a cloud router connecting all VPCs and accounts. A centralized egress VPC — containing the NAT Gateway and any inspection appliance — is attached to the Transit Gateway, and a default route in each spoke's table directs internet-bound traffic through it. This eliminates per-account NAT and centralizes egress visibility on a single inspection path. PrivateLink exposes a specific service over an interface endpoint and was not designed as a general internet-egress hub. Full-mesh VPC peering does not support transitive routing — EC2 in account A cannot reach the internet through a NAT in account B via peering alone. Provisioning a NAT Gateway in every account simply preserves the duplicate-NAT cost and inspection sprawl the security team wants to eliminate; Security Hub aggregates findings but does not perform inline traffic inspection.

questions.question: A company's EC2 instances run in a private subnet with no internet access. The instances need to read objects from an S3 bucket in the same region. The networking team wants to enable this access without deploying a NAT Gateway, which would add hourly charges and route traffic through a public endpoint. What should the engineer configure?
options: Move the EC2 instances to a public subnet and configure an S3 bucket-policy endpoint allowlist
Attach an internet gateway endpoint to the private subnet and update the route table
Add a route table entry pointing 0.0.0.0/0 at an existing VPC peering endpoint
Create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 and add a route table entry that targets it
questions.explanation: A Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 is free of charge and injects a managed prefix-list route into the subnet's route table, directing S3-bound traffic through AWS's internal network rather than the internet — satisfying both the no-NAT and no-public-endpoint requirements. Moving instances to a public subnet exposes them to inbound internet traffic and still routes S3 traffic over the public endpoint. An 'Internet Gateway endpoint' is not a real construct; an Internet Gateway is a VPC-level resource and would still require a public IP on the instance to send traffic. VPC peering connects two VPCs together at the routing layer and cannot provide a path to S3 from a peer VPC that has no internet egress.

questions.question: A security engineer at a financial services company needs all S3 buckets in the AWS account to have server-side encryption enabled at all times. When a developer creates a bucket without encryption, the configuration must be corrected automatically within minutes — without custom polling scripts. What is the most operationally efficient solution?
options: AWS CloudTrail data events that trigger a Lambda to log non-compliant buckets
Amazon EventBridge rule and a Lambda function that polls S3 bucket settings hourly
AWS Config managed rule with an SSM Automation document as the remediation action
AWS Security Hub standard with an automated response and remediation playbook
questions.explanation: AWS Config evaluates resource configurations in near-real time against managed rules such as s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled. When a rule violation is detected, an automatic remediation action invokes an SSM Automation document to enable default bucket encryption without any custom code. CloudTrail data events with a Lambda log only the non-compliant bucket — they do not remediate, and S3 bucket-creation events are management-plane events anyway, not data events. EventBridge + Lambda polling runs on a schedule rather than continuously, so it cannot meet a minutes-level detection requirement and requires custom scripting that the team wants to avoid. Security Hub aggregates security findings but does not natively remediate S3 configurations on its own.

questions.question: A security engineer is hardening an EC2 web server in a public subnet that requires SSH administration from the corporate network only (CIDR 203.0.113.0/24). All other inbound connections on port 22 must be rejected. The engineer wants the most operationally appropriate AWS-native control. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Add a Network ACL inbound allow rule for TCP 22 from 203.0.113.0/24 with a CIDR-scoped stateless security group outbound return rule
Add an inbound security group rule allowing TCP 22 from source CIDR 203.0.113.0/24
Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with an IAM policy restricting access by source IP condition
Add iptables rules on the EC2 instance to drop all TCP 22 packets sourced outside 203.0.113.0/24
questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful instance-level firewalls: an inbound allow rule for TCP 22 from 203.0.113.0/24 automatically permits the return traffic without a separate outbound rule, and the rule applies only to the specific instance — the simplest and most targeted control. A Network ACL is a stateless subnet-level firewall: an inbound allow alone is insufficient because a separate explicit outbound rule for ephemeral return ports (1024–65535) is also required, and any misconfiguration breaks SSH for every instance in the subnet. SSM Session Manager with an IAM source-IP condition replaces SSH entirely rather than restricting port 22; the IAM condition also evaluates the client's public IP, which may differ from the corporate edge CIDR after NAT, making the control fragile. iptables on the instance achieves the same result at the OS level but operates outside the AWS control plane — there's no per-instance auditability in VPC flow logs or security-group history.

questions.question: A data analytics pipeline ingests hundreds of thousands of events per second from IoT devices. Events need to be processed in real time and stored in S3 for later batch analysis. Which AWS service should anchor the ingestion layer?
options: Amazon SQS Standard with a Lambda consumer fronting the IoT device fleet for ingestion
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda or Firehose consumer for real-time ingestion
Amazon EventBridge default bus receiving IoT PutEvents calls with a Lambda processor target
Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ acting as the IoT message broker for hundreds of thousands of events
questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is designed for real-time ingestion of massive event volumes — each shard handles up to 1,000 records/second (or 1 MB/s) and shard count scales horizontally to hundreds of thousands of records per second. Records are processed in real time by Lambda or Kinesis Data Analytics while Kinesis Data Firehose ships a durable copy to S3 for batch analysis. SQS Standard is a work queue without an ordered replayable log for streaming analytics, and its per-message cost balloons at IoT-stream volumes. EventBridge enforces a 10,000 PutEvents/sec default quota and is engineered for SaaS/system events, not IoT telemetry at six-figure throughput. Amazon MQ runs traditional broker software (ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ) that is not architected to sustain hundreds of thousands of events per second.

questions.question: A healthcare startup stores de-identified patient records in S3. A new compliance framework requires (1) a verifiable log of every encryption key use, and (2) the ability to immediately revoke read access to all stored records during a security incident. The startup uses AWS KMS for key management. Which S3 server-side encryption configuration satisfies both requirements?
options: SSE-S3 using the Amazon-managed S3 key (no KMS dependency)
SSE-KMS with the aws/s3 AWS-managed KMS key for the account
SSE-KMS with a dedicated company-owned KMS key and key policy
Client-side encryption using a key fetched from AWS Secrets Manager
questions.explanation: SSE-KMS with a customer-owned KMS key records every GenerateDataKey and Decrypt call in CloudTrail, providing the verifiable key-usage log required by the compliance framework. Disabling the company-owned key immediately prevents all future decrypts of every object encrypted with it, satisfying the instant-revoke requirement. SSE-S3 uses an Amazon-managed key with no per-call CloudTrail visibility and no customer-controlled lifecycle, so neither requirement is met. The aws/s3 AWS-managed KMS key logs KMS events but is owned by AWS — the company cannot disable it, so instant revocation of all read access is impossible. Client-side encryption with a Secrets Manager key shifts encryption out of S3 entirely and doesn't generate the same S3-side audit trail; revoking access also requires rotating the secret in every client process.

questions.question: A security audit at a three-tier e-commerce company reveals that the RDS MySQL database security group permits inbound traffic on port 3306 from the entire VPC CIDR (10.0.0.0/16). The auditors require access scoped to only the application EC2 instances. An ALB forwards HTTP to an EC2 app tier, which queries the database. Which security group change satisfies least privilege with no application impact?
options: EC2 SG: inbound all from VPC CIDR; RDS SG: inbound all from VPC CIDR
EC2 SG: inbound 80 from ALB SG; RDS SG: inbound 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0
EC2 SG: inbound 80 from 0.0.0.0/0; RDS SG: inbound 3306 from any VPC instance
EC2 SG: inbound 80 from ALB SG; RDS SG: inbound 3306 from EC2 SG
questions.explanation: Referencing a security group ID in an inbound rule restricts access to exactly those instances carrying that group, updating automatically as instances scale without any IP management. EC2 SG allowing port 80 from the ALB SG accepts traffic only from the load balancer; RDS SG allowing 3306 from the EC2 SG accepts connections only from app instances, not the entire VPC CIDR that the audit flagged. Leaving the EC2 and RDS rules wide open to the VPC CIDR keeps the same over-broad access that triggered the audit finding. Allowing RDS on 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the database to the public internet — far worse than the original configuration. Allowing EC2 on port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 bypasses the ALB entirely and lets any client hit the app servers directly while still leaving RDS open to the whole VPC.

questions.question: A mobile app startup has an existing Cognito User Pool for authentication. The development team is building HTTP endpoints that invoke Lambda functions for business logic — all without maintaining EC2 instances or patching servers. The team wants token validation to happen before Lambda is invoked, with no custom authorizer code to maintain. Which AWS service combination satisfies all three constraints?
options: AWS AppSync GraphQL endpoint → Lambda resolvers → Cognito User Pool authorizer at the resolver layer
Application Load Balancer → Lambda target group → Cognito User Pool hosted-UI redirect; ALB authorizer rule
API Gateway REST API → Lambda function → Cognito User Pool Authorizer
CloudFront distribution → Lambda@Edge → custom authorizer code per edge, no user pool integration
questions.explanation: API Gateway's native Cognito User Pool Authorizer validates the JWT Bearer token in the Authorization header before routing the request to Lambda — no Lambda Authorizer code to write or maintain. AWS AppSync provides Cognito authorization but is a GraphQL endpoint, not the HTTP REST endpoints the team specified. ALB Cognito integration uses a hosted-UI redirect flow designed for browser OAuth, not a mobile API token flow; the ALB cannot validate pre-issued Bearer tokens inline and instead initiates a browser redirect, breaking mobile API clients. Lambda@Edge requires custom authorizer code in every edge function and explicitly skips user-pool integration, violating the no-custom-code constraint.

questions.question: An operations team at a regional bank runs a critical MySQL database on Amazon RDS in a single Availability Zone. During a DR test, they simulate a hardware failure in the primary AZ — recovery requires a manual restore from a daily snapshot, which takes 45 minutes and requires updating the database connection string in the application. The team's SLA mandates a 5-minute RTO with no application code changes. Which RDS configuration change achieves both requirements?
options: Promote an RDS Read Replica manually when the operations team detects the primary instance is down
RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery to a brand-new instance after failure is detected
RDS Cross-Region Read Replica with a CloudWatch alarm that triggers a Lambda-driven promotion
RDS Multi-AZ with a synchronous standby replica in a second AZ and automatic CNAME failover
questions.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby that mirrors every committed write. When the primary AZ becomes unavailable, RDS automatically promotes the standby and repoints the existing DNS CNAME within 60–120 seconds — the application reconnects through the same endpoint with no code change, meeting the 5-minute RTO. A manually promoted Read Replica requires a human-driven step and exposes a new endpoint the app must be reconfigured to use. Point-in-time recovery provisions a new instance from scratch, which routinely takes tens of minutes for a non-trivial database — and the new instance has a new endpoint, again breaking the no-code-change requirement. A cross-Region replica with alarm-triggered promotion adds replication lag plus an endpoint change, so it satisfies neither RTO nor the no-change constraint.

questions.question: A SaaS company serves 2 million active users spread across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Their REST API runs on an ALB in us-east-1, returns fully personalized responses, and cannot be cached. Which service best reduces API latency for users in distant regions?
options: Amazon CloudFront with the ALB as a custom origin
Route 53 latency-based routing directing all traffic to us-east-1
Amazon CloudFront with Lambda@Edge for per-request origin processing
AWS Global Accelerator with the ALB as an endpoint
questions.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator routes user traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge PoP, cutting the number of public-internet hops and improving TCP/TLS handshake performance for dynamic, uncacheable APIs. CloudFront is optimized for cacheable content; with fully personalized responses every request still round-trips to us-east-1, offering no consistent latency advantage over Global Accelerator. Route 53 latency-based routing selects the lowest-latency DNS record but the full TCP path still traverses the public internet to the same origin — in this case there is only one origin region anyway. CloudFront with Lambda@Edge adds per-request edge compute but, since responses cannot be cached, the origin round-trip is unavoidable; the Lambda@Edge layer just adds latency.

questions.question: A DevOps engineer with full console access accidentally runs `aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name prod-infra` during routine maintenance, taking the production environment offline for four hours. The team wants to ensure this cannot happen again without an explicit override step. Which CloudFormation safeguard directly prevents this?
options: Convert the stack to a StackSet so deletion has to be coordinated across multiple targets
Add an AWS Config rule that emits a finding when CloudFormation stack-deletion events occur
Enable drift detection on the stack so unauthorized resource changes are surfaced quickly
Enable termination protection on the production stack
questions.explanation: Termination protection causes a delete-stack API call to fail immediately — the request is rejected until an authorized user explicitly disables protection. It is the simplest direct guard against accidental stack deletion. Converting the stack to a StackSet does not gate deletion; the StackSet operations API still happily tears down stack instances. AWS Config is a detective control: it reports on deletions after they occur but cannot prevent them. Drift detection only surfaces configuration differences between live resources and the template — it has no veto on delete-stack commands.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform sends 2 million order confirmations and password-reset emails daily. The DevOps team wants to replace a self-managed Postfix relay with a fully managed AWS sending service that supports DKIM authentication, bounce and complaint processing, and delivery event notifications. Which service is the best fit?
options: Amazon SES for transactional email at scale
Amazon SNS with high-volume email subscriptions
Amazon Pinpoint for multi-channel marketing campaigns
Amazon WorkMail with programmatic API-driven sending
questions.explanation: Amazon SES is AWS's purpose-built managed email-sending service: it handles SMTP, DKIM/SPF signing, bounce and complaint feedback loops, dedicated IPs, and delivery event publishing via configuration sets — exactly the requirements the team listed. Amazon SNS email subscriptions are for simple alert notifications to human subscribers and do not perform DKIM signing or bounce handling. Pinpoint targets marketing engagement (campaigns, journeys, A/B testing) and uses SES under the hood for sending — using Pinpoint for transactional confirmations is overkill and adds segmentation features the team does not need. WorkMail is a hosted mailbox (email client + calendar) for end users, not a programmatic sending API for high volume.

questions.question: A financial services company stores sensitive compliance reports in an S3 bucket that is accessed from multiple AWS accounts within the same AWS Organization. After an internal audit, the security team needs a control that prevents any principal outside the organization from accessing the bucket — even if an IAM policy in a member account is later misconfigured. Which S3 feature most directly satisfies this requirement?
options: S3 Object Ownership set to Bucket Owner Enforced mode with no resource policy change
S3 Block Public Access policy enabled at the AWS Organization's management account
S3 bucket policy with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key
IAM permission boundary policy applied to every user across the AWS Organization
questions.explanation: A bucket policy that uses the aws:PrincipalOrgID global condition key restricts access so that only principals belonging to the specified AWS Organization can make requests, acting as an organization-wide perimeter regardless of individual IAM grants in member accounts. S3 Object Ownership in Bucket Owner Enforced mode disables ACLs and consolidates ownership but does not, by itself, prevent out-of-organization principals from accessing the bucket. IAM permission boundaries constrain what a single IAM entity can do but cannot enforce cross-account access restrictions for every account in an organization. S3 Block Public Access prevents anonymous (unauthenticated) access but does not block authenticated requests from principals outside the organization.

questions.question: An image-processing service is triggered by S3 uploads and runs on AWS Lambda. High-resolution RAW camera files have started arriving that require 22 minutes of CPU-intensive processing — seven minutes beyond Lambda's hard 15-minute execution limit. The team wants to keep a serverless approach. What is the BEST architectural fix?
options: Replace the Lambda function with an ECS Fargate task that runs the same image to bypass the timeout
Move the workload to an EC2 Auto Scaling Group with a queue-driven job pattern for long-running jobs
Increase Lambda memory to 10,240 MB and rely on the proportional vCPU bump to finish under 15 minutes
Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate Lambda invocations that each process a chunk of the image
questions.explanation: Step Functions splits a long job into stages that each fit inside Lambda's 15-minute ceiling, while the state machine handles sequencing, retries, and intermediate state — preserving the serverless model and getting around the hard timeout. ECS Fargate would also clear the timeout, but it abandons the serverless approach the team wants to keep (tasks, networking, and scaling rules now have to be managed). An EC2 Auto Scaling Group is an even larger step away from serverless and requires AMI / OS lifecycle ownership. Maxing Lambda memory to 10,240 MB speeds CPU-bound work but cannot extend the 15-minute execution ceiling, so a 22-minute job still fails.

questions.question: A startup operates 50 Lambda functions and an EC2 Auto Scaling group, all of which retrieve database credentials and API keys at startup. The security team requires KMS encryption per value, individual CloudTrail access logging, and version history for rollback. The team must store 500 config values and wants to minimize monthly AWS spend. Which service best meets all three requirements?
options: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString — KMS encryption, versioning, and CloudTrail audit
AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, KMS encryption, and $0.40 per secret per month for all 500 entries
Amazon S3 backing store with SSE-KMS encryption and per-object versioning enabled for each individual config value
Amazon DynamoDB table acting as the config store, encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key for each value
questions.explanation: Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameters are encrypted with KMS, every access is logged in CloudTrail with caller identity and parameter name, and each parameter keeps full version history — all free in the standard tier, meaning $0/month for 500 values. AWS Secrets Manager offers the same KMS encryption and audit logging plus automatic rotation, but bills $0.40 per secret per month — roughly $200/month for 500 secrets, missing the cost-minimization requirement. S3 with SSE-KMS and versioning can hold encrypted files but lacks the parameter-level fetch API, fine-grained IAM, and per-access audit semantics that secret retrieval expects. DynamoDB with a CMK is a generic key-value store; teams must build their own versioning, audit instrumentation, and access plumbing on top, multiplying operational cost.

questions.question: An e-commerce checkout API runs on an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Flash sale announcements trigger 5× traffic spikes lasting 2-3 minutes, up to 10 times daily at unpredictable times. Cold-starting a new EC2 instance from the AMI takes 4 minutes. Which Auto Scaling configuration absorbs these spikes before they cause user-visible errors?
options: Scheduled scaling actions set to each anticipated spike time
Predictive scaling using ML to forecast flash sale demand
Target tracking on ALB RequestCountPerTarget metric
Step scaling combined with a warm pool of stopped instances
questions.explanation: A warm pool holds pre-initialized EC2 instances in a Stopped state; when the step scaling policy fires, warm pool instances reach InService in seconds rather than the 4-minute cold-start time, so capacity arrives before the 2–3 minute spike ends. Step scaling adds instances in proportion to the alarm breach magnitude, scaling more aggressively when the spike is severe. Scheduled scaling fires on a calendar trigger and only helps when spike times are predictable, which the scenario explicitly rules out. Predictive scaling requires days of historical telemetry to train a forecast and assumes recurring patterns — unpredictable flash sales break that assumption. ALB RequestCountPerTarget target tracking still relies on a 4-minute cold launch, so by the time new instances are ready the spike has already produced user-visible errors.

questions.question: A company's security policy requires that IAM users cannot perform any AWS API action in the current session unless they authenticated with their MFA device — not just their password — during that session. An IAM user who logs in with only username and password must be blocked from all API calls. Which control enforces this at the API request level?
options: CloudTrail alarm firing on API calls made without MFA token
IAM Deny statement on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = false
AWS Config managed rule checking MFA activation per user
IAM password policy set to require MFA device registration
questions.explanation: An IAM policy with `Effect: Deny, Action: *` and condition `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: false` blocks all API calls in sessions where MFA was not used, regardless of what other policies allow. The user can authenticate but cannot take any action until they use their MFA device — enforcement happens at the API request level, not just at sign-in. A CloudTrail alarm is a detective control: it fires after the call has succeeded, not before, so it cannot block API actions. An AWS Config rule reports whether each user has an MFA device enabled but does not gate per-request access. An IAM password policy can require MFA device registration during account setup but does not enforce per-request MFA at the API level after login.

questions.question: A startup is migrating its monolith to about 20 containerized microservices. The platform team wants to avoid EC2 instance provisioning and Kubernetes cluster operations, and needs per-second billing for vCPU and memory consumed while each service container is running. Which compute option best fits their requirements?
options: Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type
Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type and Cluster Auto Scaling
Amazon EKS with self-managed EC2 node groups
AWS App Runner deploying containers from Amazon ECR
questions.explanation: ECS with the Fargate launch type is a serverless container engine: AWS provisions and manages the underlying compute, and you pay per vCPU-second and GB-second while tasks run — no EC2 instances to patch or scale, and per-second billing for running containers. ECS with the EC2 launch type requires provisioning and maintaining the EC2 fleet, even with Cluster Auto Scaling — the cluster instances themselves still need patching and right-sizing. EKS with self-managed node groups adds Kubernetes operational overhead on top of the same EC2 fleet management. AWS App Runner is serverless but is optimized for a single web service or API per app, not a portfolio of ~20 microservices that need service-to-service networking and orchestration.

questions.question: A company's analytics portal lets users request custom PDF reports that take 8–12 minutes to generate. The architecture must return an immediate acknowledgment to the browser, continue generating the report in the background, and notify the user via SNS when the report is ready. API Gateway has a hard 29-second integration timeout. Which pattern meets all three requirements?
options: HTTP long-poll connection held open until report finishes; user sees a spinner the whole time
Async SQS queue with worker plus an SNS completion topic that emails the user
Extend API Gateway integration timeout past 29 s; user request blocks until report is done
Browser polls a Lambda status endpoint every 10 s and shows status to the user
questions.explanation: An SQS-backed async pattern decouples the browser request from the long-running job: the frontend enqueues the request and immediately receives a job ID, a background worker processes the PDF, and SNS sends a notification when the report is ready. API Gateway's 29-second integration timeout makes a long-poll connection impossible — the proxy will close the connection long before the 8–12 minute job finishes. The integration timeout cannot be raised past 29 s, so 'extending' it is not actually a configuration option. Polling every 10 seconds works for status but wastes compute on the user's device and still requires a separate completion notification mechanism — it doesn't satisfy the immediate-acknowledgment + push-notify pattern as cleanly.

questions.question: An Aurora MySQL cluster needs to handle a sudden 10x increase in read traffic due to a promotional campaign. The write workload stays constant. What is the QUICKEST way to scale read capacity?
options: Promote a cluster read replica to a standalone writer and route reads to it
Add more Aurora Read Replicas (up to 15) to the existing cluster
Upgrade every cluster instance to a larger DB instance class
Enable Aurora Global Database to extend the cluster across regions
questions.explanation: Aurora supports up to 15 read replicas sharing the same underlying shared storage (unlike RDS replicas which each have their own copy). Adding replicas is fast and the cluster reader endpoint automatically distributes connections across them, with replica lag typically under 100 ms. Promoting a replica to a standalone writer removes it from the reader pool, reducing total read capacity rather than increasing it. Upgrading every instance to a larger class adds per-instance CPU headroom but is slower to apply, does not distribute load further, and is more expensive than fanning out small replicas. Aurora Global Database is designed for cross-region DR and read traffic in remote regions — for a single-region promotional spike it adds replication latency overhead without solving the immediate scaling problem.

questions.question: A cloud security team must deploy a standard AWS CloudTrail configuration to all 52 accounts in their AWS Organization, including accounts that join the organization in the future. Manually running scripts or console steps per account is not acceptable at this scale. Which AWS service automates this org-wide deployment?
options: AWS Config rule alerting when CloudTrail is absent per account
Lambda function calling CreateTrail across member accounts
Manual CloudFormation stack deployment in each member account
CloudFormation StackSets with Organizations integration
questions.explanation: CloudFormation StackSets with Organizations service-managed permissions automatically deploys and maintains stack instances across all accounts and regions in the organization, including any new account that joins in the future. This requires no per-account scripting and is the official AWS pattern for org-wide baseline deployments. AWS Config rules can detect missing CloudTrail and raise an alert, but Config is a detective tool — it does not deploy or remediate the trail. A Lambda function calling CreateTrail in each account is the script approach the team explicitly rejected, plus it requires custom failure-handling and account-discovery logic. Manual stack deployment per account violates the explicit 'no per-account manual steps' constraint at the scale of 52 accounts.

questions.question: A fintech company stores payment transactions in DynamoDB. For regulatory compliance, every item modification must be captured in an immutable audit log showing both the old and new attribute values. The solution must not require changes to the existing application, which writes directly to DynamoDB. Which approach creates a complete item-level change history?
options: DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery with hourly snapshot comparisons
DynamoDB Streams consumed by Lambda, writing events to S3
DynamoDB on-demand backup job triggered by an EventBridge rule
DynamoDB Global Tables replicating to an audit-only AWS region
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams records every INSERT, MODIFY, and REMOVE event at the item level, including both the old and new attribute images, with no changes needed in the writing application. A Lambda function triggered by the stream writes each event record to S3 (with a Glacier or Object Lock layer for immutability), creating a per-modification audit trail. Point-in-Time Recovery lets you restore the entire table to a past moment but does not expose a log of individual change events. Global Tables replicate data across regions for active-active access without tracking what changed. On-demand backups capture full table snapshots rather than per-modification records, so the team would have to diff entire tables to reconstruct change history.

questions.question: A genomics company runs a batch analysis pipeline on EC2 that processes 3 TB of sequencing data per job, taking 8-12 hours. The pipeline saves progress to S3 every 15 minutes and resumes from the last checkpoint after any failure. Jobs must complete eventually but have no hard deadline. Which EC2 purchasing option minimizes compute cost for this workload?
options: Spot Instances with restart-from-checkpoint after any reclamation event
On-Demand Instances billed per second with no commitment so capacity is always available immediately
Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year all-upfront payment plan for the deepest committed-use discount
Dedicated Hosts under a 1-year term to guarantee dedicated underlying capacity for the batch fleet always
questions.explanation: Spot Instances are priced up to ~90% below On-Demand rates, and the pipeline's 15-minute checkpointing makes it tolerant of the 2-minute Spot reclamation notice — when an instance is reclaimed, the job resumes from the last S3 checkpoint with minimal rework. On-Demand pays full per-second pricing with no discount; it works but is the most expensive option for an interruptible workload. Standard Reserved Instances offer steep savings on steady-state usage but commit the bill regardless of whether the batch is running, leaving idle reservations between jobs. Dedicated Hosts are reserved physical servers priced for software-licensing compliance, the most expensive per-hour option here.

questions.question: A SaaS company wants to enforce HTTPS on its public web application. Users who access the plain HTTP URL in their browser should automatically be sent to the HTTPS version. The change must be applied at the load balancer with no modifications to the application servers. Which load balancer type and configuration achieves this?
options: Network Load Balancer with TCP 80→443 forwarding for application users
Classic Load Balancer with HTTP listener and SSL offloading for application users
Gateway Load Balancer with inline forwarding rules applied to user traffic
Application Load Balancer with an HTTP listener redirect action for users
questions.explanation: Application Load Balancer is the only AWS load balancer that can inspect Layer-7 HTTP content and respond with a redirect action — for example, returning an HTTP 301 on port 80 that points the browser to the HTTPS endpoint on port 443. This is configured as a listener rule on the port-80 listener and involves no backend instances. Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP) and cannot read or modify HTTP headers, so it cannot issue a protocol-level redirect. Classic Load Balancer supports SSL termination but lacks listener rule actions for HTTP→HTTPS redirects. Gateway Load Balancer is for transparent insertion of L3 inspection appliances (firewalls/IDS), not for L7 client-facing HTTP termination or redirect logic.

questions.question: A bank's compliance team must ensure that API audit logs shipped to an S3 bucket cannot be modified or deleted by anyone — including administrators and the root account — before a mandatory 90-day hold expires. They also need cryptographic proof that each log file has not been altered since delivery. Which two controls together satisfy both requirements?
options: Enable CloudTrail log file validation and apply S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode
Enable S3 MFA Delete and bucket versioning so each log file's prior versions cannot be removed
Encrypt every log file with a KMS CMK and restrict key use to the compliance team
Add a bucket policy Deny on s3:DeleteObject for all IAM principals covering every log file in the bucket
questions.explanation: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode creates a WORM hold that even the root account cannot override before the retention period ends, satisfying the deletion-prevention requirement. CloudTrail log file validation generates an hourly SHA-256 digest chain; any post-delivery tampering breaks the chain and is immediately detectable, providing the cryptographic integrity proof. S3 MFA Delete + versioning can be disabled by the root user, so it does not provide the same ironclad guarantee as Object Lock Compliance mode. KMS encryption protects confidentiality but not integrity — an administrator with key access could still delete the objects, and there is no per-file integrity attestation. A bucket policy Deny on s3:DeleteObject can be removed by an admin with bucket-policy write permission, leaving no irrevocable retention guarantee.

questions.question: A company's e-commerce platform is fully stateless and handles flash sales that spike traffic to 10× normal within 30 seconds. The infrastructure team cannot reliably pre-warm capacity for unpredictable sale windows. Which compute approach meets the sub-minute scaling requirement?
options: EC2 Auto Scaling with target-tracking scaling on CPU
AWS Lambda behind an Application Load Balancer
A pre-sized On-Demand EC2 fleet reserved for peak load
Elastic Beanstalk with time-based scheduled scale-out
questions.explanation: AWS Lambda scales from zero to thousands of concurrent executions in seconds without provisioning or warm-up delays, making it ideal for a stateless workload facing unpredictable sub-minute traffic spikes. EC2 Auto Scaling with CPU target tracking typically takes 3–5 minutes to launch and initialize new instances — far slower than the 30-second surge window. Elastic Beanstalk scheduled scale-out requires knowing when the surge will happen, which the scenario explicitly rules out. A pre-sized On-Demand EC2 fleet covers the spike but wastes cost during normal load and is not a 'scaling approach' so much as static over-provisioning.

questions.question: A financial company's on-premises Oracle 19c database is written to 24/7 and must be migrated to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with fewer than 4 hours of application downtime. The database is 2 TB. Which migration approach satisfies this requirement?
options: Oracle Data Pump export/import into Aurora PostgreSQL during a scheduled maintenance window
AWS DMS with CDC replication into Aurora PostgreSQL
AWS Snowball physical transfer of the 2 TB Oracle export, then a one-shot load into Aurora PostgreSQL
AWS SCT schema conversion to Aurora PostgreSQL only, with no data-replication tier
questions.explanation: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) performs a full initial load, then uses Change Data Capture (CDC) to replicate ongoing transactions to the Aurora PostgreSQL target while the Oracle source remains online — shrinking the cutover window to minutes, well within the 4-hour downtime budget. Oracle Data Pump requires pausing writes during export, which is incompatible with a 24/7 source database of 2 TB. AWS Snowball physically transports bulk data but provides no live-replication tier — the source must still be paused during the final load, exceeding the downtime constraint. AWS Schema Conversion Tool converts schemas and code objects but does not migrate the data itself, so it must be paired with DMS.

questions.question: An enterprise manages a central networking account containing a VPC with carefully segmented subnets. Twenty application accounts in the same AWS Organization need to deploy EC2 instances and RDS clusters using those centrally managed subnets, without owning their own VPCs. Which AWS capability enables this?
options: AWS Transit Gateway with cross-account attachments so each spoke account can deploy resources into centrally managed subnets via accounts sharing
VPC Peering from the hub account to each spoke account's own VPC and subnets
AWS Resource Access Manager sharing the centrally managed subnets across accounts
AWS PrivateLink endpoint services per spoke VPC, each spoke owning its own subnets
questions.explanation: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) lets the subnet-owning account share specific subnets with participant accounts in the same AWS Organization. Participants can launch EC2, RDS, and other resources directly into those shared subnets while the network team retains control of routing, NACLs, and security groups. AWS Transit Gateway interconnects separate VPCs at the routing level but does not let participant accounts deploy resources into a subnet that lives in a different account's VPC. VPC Peering links two separate VPCs without granting subnet-level deployment access in the peer account. PrivateLink exposes a specific service endpoint and is not a mechanism for sharing entire subnets.

questions.question: A SaaS provider runs a payment-processing API inside their AWS VPC. A customer company wants to invoke that API from within their own VPC without traversing the internet, without CIDR overlap constraints, and without gaining access to any other resource in the provider's VPC. Which networking pattern satisfies all three requirements?
options: VPC Peering between provider and customer accounts
AWS Transit Gateway connecting both company VPCs
AWS Direct Connect dedicated link to the provider
AWS PrivateLink backed by a Network Load Balancer
questions.explanation: AWS PrivateLink creates an Interface VPC Endpoint in the consumer's VPC that maps to a VPC Endpoint Service backed by a Network Load Balancer in the provider's VPC. Traffic stays within the AWS network, CIDR ranges never need to align, and the consumer can only reach that specific NLB — not the rest of the provider's VPC. VPC Peering grants full network-level routing between the two VPCs, violating the isolation requirement, and it fails outright if CIDR ranges overlap. Transit Gateway also enables broad cross-VPC routing rather than service-scoped access. Direct Connect is a private link between on-premises and AWS, not between two AWS VPCs in different accounts.

questions.question: A team's serverless checkout API runs on API Gateway backed by Lambda. During a flash sale, multiple functions in the same AWS account exhaust the shared regional concurrency pool, leaving the checkout function throttled while lower-priority background functions remain active. The team wants to guarantee the checkout function always has a minimum concurrency allocation that other functions in the account cannot claim. Which Lambda feature addresses this?
options: Reserved concurrency set on the checkout Lambda function
Provisioned concurrency for the checkout Lambda function
AWS Lambda Power Tuning to reduce per-invocation duration
API Gateway usage plan throttling per customer API key
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency carves out a dedicated slice of the account-level concurrency pool exclusively for the specified function. Other functions cannot consume that reserved portion, ensuring the checkout function is never starved by lower-priority workloads competing for the shared pool. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments to eliminate cold starts but does not prevent other functions from consuming the unreserved portion of the account-wide limit, so checkout can still be throttled at peak. Lambda Power Tuning helps right-size memory for per-invocation cost/latency but does not guarantee minimum concurrent capacity. API Gateway usage plans throttle individual external API keys but have no effect on how Lambda allocates its internal concurrency pool across functions.

questions.question: A data engineering team stores 18 months of clickstream logs in Amazon S3 as Parquet files partitioned by date. Business analysts need to run ad-hoc SQL queries against this data without provisioning a database cluster or building ETL pipelines. Which service meets this need at the lowest operational overhead?
options: Amazon Redshift Spectrum reading S3 Parquet directly
Amazon Athena querying via the Glue Data Catalog
Amazon EMR Spark cluster querying the S3 dataset
AWS Glue Studio ETL job loading S3 data to DynamoDB
questions.explanation: Amazon Athena is fully serverless — analysts write standard SQL and Athena reads Parquet files directly from S3 using the Glue Data Catalog for schema and partition information, with no cluster to provision or maintain. Redshift Spectrum also queries S3 directly but requires a running Redshift cluster to issue queries, adding provisioning and management overhead. Amazon EMR Spark provides distributed processing power but requires launching and operating a cluster of EC2 nodes (or a serverless EMR application that is still more complex than Athena). AWS Glue Studio is a data-transformation tool that loads data into a target store; it is not an ad-hoc SQL interface against S3 — and writing the clickstream into DynamoDB would not even support the analytical query patterns the team needs.

questions.question: A financial services company operates 14 AWS accounts under a single AWS Organization. Developers authenticate through IAM Identity Center (SSO). The CISO must prove to auditors that every administrative API call—including calls made through federated IAM Identity Center sessions—is logged centrally and cannot be tampered with by individual account owners. Which single solution satisfies both requirements?
options: Deploy an AWS Config Organization aggregator with Conformance Packs enabled in every member account
Set up cross-account CloudWatch Logs subscriptions routing application logs from each member to a central hub
Enable VPC Flow Logs in every member account and stream the results to a centralized S3 bucket
Create a CloudTrail Organization Trail writing events to a log-archive S3 bucket
questions.explanation: A CloudTrail Organization Trail automatically enables CloudTrail in every member account and delivers all management-plane API events — including IAM Identity Center assumed-role calls — to a central S3 bucket in a log-archive account that individual account owners cannot modify. An AWS Config aggregator captures resource configuration state and compliance posture, not API-call records, so it cannot prove every administrative call was logged. Cross-account CloudWatch Logs subscriptions require per-service configuration and capture application logs, not the AWS management-plane API events the CISO needs. VPC Flow Logs record network-traffic metadata only — they contain no information about who called which AWS API.

questions.question: A fintech company's SOC 2 audit requires that third-party auditors, who operate their own separate AWS account, have read-only access to specific S3 buckets for a two-week review window. The security team's constraints are: no long-lived credentials may be created, and no bucket endpoint may be exposed to the public internet. What should they configure?
options: Create an IAM user per auditor and email the access keys to each
Create a cross-account IAM role and share its ARN with the auditors
Share presigned S3 URLs (2-week expiry) directly with each auditor
Create a new AWS account for auditors and assign root-level S3 access
questions.explanation: A cross-account IAM role with an S3 read-only policy and a trust policy scoped to the auditor's AWS account lets the auditors call sts:AssumeRole to obtain short-lived temporary credentials — no long-lived keys are created or shared. Deleting the role at the end of the review instantly revokes all access. Creating an IAM user per auditor and emailing access keys produces long-lived credentials that may be forwarded or cached, violating the no-permanent-credentials requirement. Creating a new AWS account just for auditors with root-level S3 access grants far more privilege than required and creates a long-lived shared account. Presigned URLs are publicly accessible HTTPS endpoints — anyone who holds the URL can fetch the object — and cannot be scoped to a specific external AWS account, failing both security constraints.

questions.question: A Lambda function reads 15 SSM Parameter Store values synchronously on every invocation. During peak traffic the function runs 800 times per minute, causing ThrottlingException errors from SSM as the default throughput quota is exceeded. The team wants the most effective fix for the throttling without moving configuration to a different service. What should the architect recommend?
options: Embed all 15 parameters as Lambda environment variables to remove SSM dependency entirely
Upgrade to Parameter Store Advanced tier to raise the regional API throughput limit to 1,000 TPS
Replace SSM Parameter Store with AWS AppConfig and leverage its native client-side polling and caching
Cache retrieved parameters in the Lambda execution environment and refresh them on a TTL
questions.explanation: Lambda execution contexts persist across warm invocations. Caching parameter values in a module-level variable with a short TTL (5–10 minutes) means each execution context fetches from SSM only once per interval instead of on every invocation, reducing API call volume by orders of magnitude and eliminating the throttling. Baking parameters into Lambda environment variables also stops the SSM calls but prevents runtime rotation without a Lambda deployment — and the question explicitly wants to keep configuration in SSM. Upgrading to Parameter Store Advanced tier raises the throughput ceiling but adds cost without fixing the root cause: 800 invocations × 15 parameters = 12,000 calls/minute is wasteful regardless of the quota. Migrating to AWS AppConfig violates the no-different-service constraint.

questions.question: A media company built a proprietary transcoding engine that runs as a Docker container. Videos averaging 15 minutes of processing time are uploaded to S3 at a rate of several thousand per day. The team wants transcoding workers to scale automatically with upload volume and pay only for compute used while jobs run. Which architecture best meets these requirements?
options: Trigger a Lambda function from each S3 upload event and stream the transcode output back to S3
EC2 On-Demand Auto Scaling group pulling jobs from an SQS queue with a custom AMI per worker
ECS Fargate tasks consuming an SQS queue, with Application Auto Scaling driven by queue depth
Step Functions parallel states that launch one EC2 instance per upload and tear it down after the transcode
questions.explanation: S3 event notifications publish to SQS; ECS Fargate tasks dequeue and process jobs, with Application Auto Scaling adjusting task count based on ApproximateNumberOfMessages. Fargate comfortably handles 15-minute (and much longer) jobs and bills per second of vCPU/memory while tasks run — paying only for compute used. Lambda's 15-minute invocation ceiling equals the average job duration, so longer videos time out outright. EC2 On-Demand Auto Scaling can run the workload but introduces AMI lifecycle, OS patching, and idle-fleet cost between scaling events. Step Functions launching an EC2 per video pays minutes of provisioning latency per job and is hugely expensive at thousands of videos per day.

questions.question: A fintech startup's web API sits behind an Application Load Balancer. A penetration test finds the application is vulnerable to injection attacks via crafted HTTP query strings and request bodies. The CISO wants a control that inspects Layer 7 HTTP content and blocks malicious request patterns before they reach the EC2 backend — without modifying the application code. Which service should the team attach directly to the ALB?
options: Amazon GuardDuty with VPC Flow Logs and DNS threat detection for the web tier
AWS Network Firewall deployed in a dedicated inspection VPC in front of the web ALB
AWS WAF with managed rule groups for common web exploits
AWS Shield Advanced with proactive DDoS response engagement for the web fleet
questions.explanation: AWS WAF attaches directly to an ALB (or CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync) and inspects HTTP request headers, URI, query strings, and body against rule groups — including the AWS Managed Rules set for common web exploits (SQLi, XSS, path traversal). Rules can block matching requests before they reach the backend, with no application code changes. GuardDuty is a threat-detection service that analyzes logs and network metadata to surface findings; it does not block HTTP traffic in real time. AWS Network Firewall operates at the VPC perimeter and inspects network traffic but does not attach to an ALB or inspect HTTP payloads at the same Layer-7 granularity. Shield Advanced mitigates volumetric DDoS attacks at Layers 3 and 4 and is not designed for blocking application-layer injection patterns.

questions.question: A three-tier e-commerce application runs web servers, app servers, and an RDS MySQL database in separate subnets. A security audit finds the RDS instance accepts connections on port 3306 from the full VPC CIDR (10.0.0.0/16). The team must restrict database access to only the app-tier EC2 instances in a way that remains accurate as instances are replaced or the fleet scales without manual IP updates. What should they configure?
options: Update the RDS security group to allow port 3306 from the app-tier subnet CIDR
