Reference the app-tier security group in the RDS security group inbound rule
Apply a subnet NACL on the RDS subnet blocking all traffic except from the app-tier subnet
Move the RDS instance to an isolated VPC and connect it to the app-tier via PrivateLink
questions.explanation: Referencing the app-tier security group ID in the RDS security group's inbound rule grants access to all instances carrying that group at the time of each request — when app-tier instances are replaced or scale out, new EC2s inherit the security group and immediately gain database access without any manual rule update. Allowing 3306 from the app-tier subnet CIDR also permits any other EC2 launched into that subnet — monitoring agents, developer tools, or a compromised instance — not just the app-tier application. NACLs are stateless: an inbound allow for 3306 also requires an explicit outbound rule covering ephemeral ports (1024–65535), doubling maintenance overhead and increasing the chance of misconfiguration. Moving RDS to an isolated VPC reachable only via PrivateLink is functional but heavy-weight overkill that introduces an extra endpoint and per-connection cost when an SG-to-SG reference already enforces the same isolation.

questions.question: A media company's BI team runs nightly reports that JOIN a 3 TB fact table against several dimension tables with multi-level GROUP BY aggregations spanning 18 months of history. Queries currently take 45-90 minutes on an Aurora MySQL instance and leadership wants them under 5 minutes. Which AWS service is architecturally best suited for this workload?
options: Amazon DynamoDB with Global Secondary Indexes for high-throughput key lookups
Amazon Athena querying Parquet files stored in an S3 data lake
Amazon Redshift with columnar storage and MPP query execution
Amazon Aurora MySQL with additional read replicas for query offloading
questions.explanation: Amazon Redshift uses columnar storage and massively parallel processing (MPP) across multiple nodes, making it ideal for complex multi-table JOINs and large aggregations at terabyte-to-petabyte scale — queries that take 45–90 minutes on a row-based OLTP engine typically complete in seconds to a few minutes on a properly sized Redshift cluster. DynamoDB's key-value model does not support SQL-style JOINs or GROUP BY aggregations at all. Amazon Athena suits ad-hoc exploration but query performance on heavy multi-table JOINs is less predictable than a dedicated MPP warehouse, especially when the same query is rerun nightly. Aurora MySQL read replicas distribute OLTP read load but do not change the row-scan architecture that makes large analytical aggregations slow.

questions.question: A web application runs on an EC2 instance with an instance profile granting s3:* on all resources and ec2:* on all resources. A security review shows the application only ever performs object retrieval from a single S3 bucket named 'prod-assets'. The team wants to reduce the blast radius if the instance is compromised. Which IAM change should a solutions architect implement?
options: Add an explicit Deny on s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject for prod-assets and remove ec2:* assets to limit scope
Remove ec2:* entirely and replace s3:* with s3:GetObject scoped to the 'prod-assets' bucket ARN
Attach a permissions boundary that limits the instance to S3 read-only on any bucket
Enable IAM Access Analyzer and archive bucket findings for the instance profile
questions.explanation: Least privilege requires granting only the exact permissions actually needed. Removing ec2:* entirely (the application makes no EC2 API calls) and replacing s3:* with s3:GetObject on the specific bucket ARN directly eliminates the excess permissions and shrinks the blast radius if the instance is compromised. Adding Deny statements for selected S3 writes is weaker — the broad s3:* Allow remains, so any new S3 API added by AWS in the future is automatically granted until someone updates the policy. A permissions boundary constrains the ceiling of what the role could be granted, but does not remove the existing broad Allow inside the role's policy. IAM Access Analyzer flags overly permissive findings but does not modify the underlying policy.

questions.question: A company runs an active-passive disaster-recovery configuration across two AWS regions. The RTO target is 15 minutes and the RPO target is 1 minute. The operations team is evaluating database replication options for the primary workload. Which approach can reliably meet the RPO target?
options: RDS automated database snapshots replicated hourly to the secondary region
RDS Multi-AZ standby database with automatic failover, primary region only
RDS cross-region read replica database promoted manually on failure
Aurora Global Database with an always-on secondary database cluster
questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates data to a secondary region with typical latency under one second — well within the 1-minute RPO — using dedicated replication infrastructure independent of the database engine, and a managed regional failover meets a 15-minute RTO. RDS automated snapshots are taken at most hourly, yielding an RPO of up to 60 minutes, which far exceeds the 1-minute target. RDS Multi-AZ provides high availability within a single region via synchronous replication to a standby but does not address cross-region DR. RDS cross-region read replicas use asynchronous engine-level replication whose lag can exceed one minute under sustained write load, making RPO compliance unreliable.

questions.question: An operations team manages EC2 instances in private subnets with no NAT gateway or internet gateway. The instances run SSM Agent for patch management, call the EC2 API for resource discovery, and assume IAM roles via STS. All three functions have stopped working because there is no path to the AWS public endpoints. The security policy prohibits adding a NAT gateway to avoid routing AWS API traffic over the public internet. What must a solutions architect configure?
options: Create Interface VPC Endpoints for Systems Manager, EC2, and STS in the relevant subnets
Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet and add a default route from the private subnets to the NAT gateway
Configure Gateway VPC Endpoints for SSM, EC2, and STS, which are available for all AWS services
Launch a proxy EC2 instance in a public subnet and configure the private instances to relay API calls through it
questions.explanation: Interface VPC Endpoints (powered by AWS PrivateLink) create ENIs in the private subnet that route traffic to the AWS service over the AWS backbone — no internet required. SSM, EC2, and STS all support Interface Endpoints. A NAT Gateway is explicitly prohibited by the security policy because it routes AWS API traffic over the public internet. Gateway Endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB; they cannot be created for SSM, EC2, or STS, so claiming they work for 'all AWS services' is factually incorrect. A self-managed proxy EC2 in a public subnet still sends API traffic over the public internet on its egress side and introduces a single point of failure that violates the no-internet requirement.

questions.question: A financial services firm must satisfy a compliance mandate that all AWS API activity — including read-only calls — be retained for 7 years with cryptographic proof that no log has been altered or deleted after delivery. The team routes logs to a dedicated S3 archive bucket. Which combination of CloudTrail and S3 settings satisfies all three requirements?
options: CloudTrail log file validation; S3 Standard storage with a 7-year lifecycle rule meeting the compliance retention
S3 MFA Delete plus versioning; Standard-IA with a 7-year lifecycle rule documented in the compliance binder
CloudTrail log file validation; S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year hold
KMS CMK encryption for each log; Glacier Deep Archive with a 7-year compliance expiry policy
questions.explanation: CloudTrail log file validation generates an hourly SHA-256 digest chain; any modification to a log file or its digest after delivery breaks the chain, providing cryptographic proof of integrity. S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode creates a WORM hold for the full retention period that even the root account cannot override, guaranteeing 7-year immutability. The first option enables log file validation but stores objects in S3 Standard without Object Lock — an administrator can still delete the files, failing the deletion-prevention requirement. MFA Delete plus a lifecycle rule can be disabled by the root account, and a 'compliance binder' is paperwork, not a technical control. KMS encryption with Deep Archive protects confidentiality but not integrity — a user with key access could still delete objects, and Deep Archive's compliance-tier expiry policy is not a substitute for Object Lock immutability.

questions.question: A development team is decomposing a monolithic order platform into ECS Fargate microservices. The checkout flow must call an inventory service to verify stock and a payments service to charge the customer—in sequence—before returning a confirmation to the user. Both downstream calls must complete before the response is sent, and the end-to-end latency budget is 80 ms within the same VPC. Which communication architecture should the team adopt?
options: Expose both downstream services behind an internal Application Load Balancer with path-based routing
Connect each service pair with an Amazon SQS FIFO queue using a correlation ID and a reply queue
Publish each request to an SNS topic and let the downstream service deliver the result via a second topic
Stream calls through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with one shard per service to preserve ordering
questions.explanation: An internal Application Load Balancer provides synchronous request-response semantics inside the VPC, with path-based routing to separate ECS target groups for inventory and payments. Round-trips over an internal ALB are typically single-digit milliseconds, comfortably within the 80 ms budget for two sequential calls. SQS is asynchronous — bolting on a correlation ID and reply queue introduces polling and queue latency that blows the budget. SNS is pub/sub fan-out, not request-response, and a two-topic acknowledgment dance still relies on polling. Kinesis is built for ordered event streaming with consumer-driven polling, not synchronous RPC-style calls between microservices.
